archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (goaltending-sunk)
archetype.definition: A Sabres team that controls 5-on-5 play like a top-half club but sits 26th on the site because its goalies and both special-teams units are giving away the margin.

report.headline: Out-chancing teams nightly, undone by .861 goaltending and broken special teams
report.take:
Buffalo is coming off its best season in this five-year window: 109 points, the site's 5th-ranked team and seven playoff wins. Nine games into 2026-27 it sits 26th on the Teams tab with a -7 goal differential, the 28th-worst goals-against rate in the league and a 91-point pace. Read only the standings and goal differential and this looks like a step back. The 5-on-5 numbers say otherwise.

At even strength the Sabres are pushing play. Their 54% CF % ranks 7th, their .525 xGF % ranks 13th, and they allow fewer shots a game than the league average. The blueline grades A- and is doing most of that work. Owen Power logs 26.75 minutes a night at a .580 xGF %, and Mattias Samuelsson and Olen Zellweger are also well above water. The losses come from three places that have nothing to do with territory: an .861 team save percentage (30th), a 9.1% power play (dead last) and a 64.5% penalty kill (30th). PDO of 97.7 at 5-on-5 and 97.3 in all situations tells you the bounces have gone against them. The shooting is league-average, so nearly all of that shortfall is in net.

There is luck on the other side of the ledger too. Their Pts vs Goal Diff of +2 ranks 2nd in the league, a lot of overtime games have banked loser points, and that is why 4-3-2 looks better than a -7 differential. The good news hiding in the bad goaltending is that it isn't evenly spread. Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen is at -4.3 GSAx over six starts, while Colten Ellis is roughly average at +0.2. Last season's team goaltending saved 24.5 goals above expected, so this is a collapse from a strong baseline, not a known weakness.

The forward group is thinner than the blueline. Tage Thompson and Jack Quinn have five goals each, and Zach Benson is driving play at .643 xGF % with six assists and no goals yet. Below the top four, though, McLeod, Norris, Krebs and Helenius are all under water by xGF % and minus by +/-. That middle-six weakness is why the forwards grade only C. Expect the save percentage and the penalty kill to drift back toward normal and the overtime luck to fade. The net should be a team that climbs well above 26th.

strengths.title: Owning 5-on-5 possession
strengths.body: Buffalo takes 54% of the shot attempts and more than half the expected goals at even strength, both comfortably above league average. It also allows fewer shots on goal than the league does. This is the most stable kind of number in hockey, and it says the process is sound even while the scoreboard disagrees.

strengths.title: An A- blueline led by Power
strengths.body: Power carries nearly 27 minutes a night with a .580 xGF % and eight points, ranking 11th among defensemen on the site. Samuelsson and Zellweger give the top four real depth. Rasmus Dahlin has played only six of the nine games and still has two power-play points, so the group has room to get better as his minutes fill in.

strengths.title: Top line producing at both ends
strengths.body: Thompson and Quinn have nine points each, and Quinn leads the forwards in Game Score. Benson's .643 xGF % says the chances are coming even though he has yet to score. With league-average team shooting, there is no finishing bubble here to pop.

concerns.title: Goaltending is bleeding goals
concerns.body: An .861 save percentage ranks 30th, against a league average of .893. Team GSAx is -4.6, and nearly all of it belongs to Luukkonen's -4.3. It is also why opposing forwards are outscoring their expected points by more against Buffalo than against anyone else. A team that saved 24.5 goals above expected last year should not stay this low, but until Luukkonen steadies, the starts question is real.

concerns.title: Special teams at the league floor
concerns.body: The power play converts 9.1%, last in the league and more than 11 points below average. The penalty kill at 64.5% is 30th. Both are tiny samples over nine games and both should rise. Until they do, a team winning at 5-on-5 keeps handing back its edge whenever a whistle goes.

concerns.title: Record propped by overtime points
concerns.body: A Pts vs Goal Diff of +2, 2nd in the league, means the standings are kinder than the goal differential. Overtime results tend to even out. Part of the expected improvement in goal margin will therefore be offset by fewer cheap points.

trend.note: October has been a back-and-forth 4-5 month with no streak longer than two games either way. The last five games produced a .600 points percentage and 3.4 goals a game, slightly better than the season rate, but they kept allowing nearly four a night.

weekAhead.headline: Two soft opponents and a PDO-fueled Capitals team in between
weekAhead.body:
Philadelphia comes to Buffalo at 1-6-3 with the league's worst xGF % (.34) and CF % (.41). It is also last in shots against, giving up 32.8 a game. If the Sabres win the territory battle, they should win it by a lot here. The catch is that Flyers goaltending has been good, at +4.1 GSAx, so the shot volume needs to turn into goals.

The trip then goes to Washington and San Jose. The Capitals are 5-3-0 and 10th on the site, but they are being carried by a 104.1 PDO and +7.4 goalie GSAx while taking only 45% of the shot attempts. Buffalo's possession edge should travel against them. San Jose is 4-3-1 on the league-best Pts vs Goal Diff, with a .408 xGF % and an .877 save percentage behind it. Two of these three opponents give Buffalo's process every chance to show up on the scoreboard.

keyMatchups.title: Shot volume versus the Flyers
keyMatchups.body: Philadelphia allows the most shots in the league and generates almost nothing at 5-on-5. Its .902 save percentage is the only thing keeping games close. This is the clearest spot on the schedule for Buffalo's attack to break out.

keyMatchups.title: Washington's hot hand in net
keyMatchups.body: The Capitals' record rests on a 104.1 PDO and a +7.4 goalie GSAx, not on possession. Buffalo should hold the puck, but it may need its own goalie to match Washington's to take points in this one.

keyMatchups.title: San Jose's luck versus soft goaltending
keyMatchups.body: The Sharks lead the league in points beyond their goal differential while getting badly out-chanced. Their .877 save percentage gives Buffalo's shooters a real target. This is a game the Sabres should control.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in net, and whether Luukkonen's save percentage climbs off .860, against two opponents that shoot poorly.

restOfSeason.body:
The parts of this team that tend to last are good: possession, shot suppression and a deep, A- blueline. The parts sinking it are the ones that swing most over nine games: save percentage, power-play conversion and penalty-kill rate. Expect all three to move toward league norms, which should turn a goal differential pacing for -64 into something close to even or slightly positive. Against that, a +2 overtime cushion that ranks 2nd will likely fade.

This still doesn't look like last year's 109-point team, because the forward depth behind the top four is weak and the goaltending has gone from an asset to a question mark. The projection is a points total around or a bit above the current 91-point pace, with goals against falling meaningfully. That keeps them in the Atlantic playoff race rather than out of it.
swingFactors: Luukkonen's save percentage, or a shift of starts to Ellis
Power play and penalty kill recovering toward league average

confidence.note: Nine games: possession is fairly telling already, but goaltending and special-teams rates are mostly noise this early.
